screens.title: Distributed Data Management (Simplified)
screens.narratorSegment: Managing data across microservices is one of the hardest practical problems in distributed systems. In this chapter you will learn why a shared monolithic database undermines service autonomy, what it means for each service to own its database, how different consistency models affect user experience, and a pragmatic pattern — the Saga — for coordinating multi-step business processes. We'll use the order fulfillment example to see events, local transactions, and compensating operations in action, and we'll practice designing a small saga for user registration. By the end you should be able to pick appropriate consistency levels, explain the trade-offs of database-per-service, and outline a saga that keeps the system reliable without locking all services into a single transaction. A common misconception is that distributed ACID transactions are always the safest choice; we'll explain why they often reduce availability and how sagas offer a more operationally practical alternative. Think of this chapter as a map: you will learn patterns and pitfalls so you can choose the simplest safe approach for your business needs.

screens.title: Monolith shared database vs Database per Service
screens.narratorSegment: Start by contrasting two basic approaches: a single shared database for all components, and database-per-service where each microservice owns its private store. In a monolith, components read and write the same schema, so transactions are easy: a single ACID commit enforces correctness. That sounds convenient, but it tightly couples teams, deployment cycles, and schema changes. A migration or an index change can force coordinated releases across multiple teams. Conversely, database-per-service enforces strong service boundaries. Each service controls its schema, technology, and scaling, enabling independent deployments. An immediate benefit is polyglot persistence: you can pick a document database for flexible product catalogs and a relational database for payments. The trade-off is that multi-service business operations no longer fit into one ACID transaction. You must design coordination protocols and accept potential temporary inconsistencies. A common misconception is that autonomy implies data duplication is wrong; in fact, duplicating data across services is often the practical path to resilience. Example: an Order service keeps its own order records while Inventory service keeps stock counts; both may store the same product ID but each maintains the data it needs. Key takeaway: prefer autonomy for rapid delivery, but plan explicit coordination for cross-service consistency. Which boundaries in your system are worth strict coupling, and which deserve independent evolution?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Monolith vs Database per Service
Monolithic shared database
Single schema, single commit, global ACID transactions. Easy consistency but high coupling across teams and deployments.
  • Strong consistency by default through ACID transactions.
  • Tight coupling: schema changes require coordination.
  • Scaling is monolithic and global rather than per-service.
Common mistake
Attempting to keep microservices but retaining a shared DB preserves coupling and undermines the benefits of microservices.
Database per service
Each service owns its private database. Services communicate by APIs or events; no direct DB access between services.
  • Loose coupling and independent deployments.
  • Polyglot persistence: pick the right store per service.
  • Requires explicit coordination for cross-service operations.
Pro tip
Design clear boundaries; replicate only the minimal data needed for performance or availability.
Example
Product service uses a document store for flexible attributes while Payment service uses a relational store for transactional integrity.
Scenario
An order creation touches three databases; plan how to coordinate those changes without blocking services.
Key Takeaway

Prefer service-owned databases for autonomy, but design explicit coordination for multi-service transactions.

screens.title: Database per Service
screens.narratorSegment: Database per service means each microservice owns and controls its own private datastore; other services never access that store directly. This enforces service autonomy: each team can deploy, scale, and evolve schema without coordinating changes across unrelated teams. The benefits include loose coupling, technology choice per service (polyglot persistence), and localized performance tuning. A practical example: ProductService uses a document database to store variable product attributes and support flexible queries; PaymentService uses a relational database to rely on ACID semantics for money transfers. Importantly, ownership implies responsibility: the owning service must provide APIs or events for others to access its data. A typical misconception is that owning a private database removes the need to think about global data; it does not. You still need to design APIs, decide what to duplicate, and plan for eventual consistency when data is replicated. Also consider operational costs: multiple datastores may increase run-time maintenance and monitoring. A short checklist helps: define the canonical data owner, expose minimal read APIs or events, make replicated fields eventually consistent, and design idempotent update operations. Practical takeaway: use database-per-service to preserve team autonomy, but invest in clear contracts and monitoring so cross-service data flows remain reliable.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Database-per-service grants ownership and autonomy; it requires deliberate API and event design to keep systems consistent and observable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Database per Service
Database per service
A service owns a private database and publishes its data via API or events. No other service reads or writes that database directly.
Benefit: Loose coupling
Teams can deploy independently and evolve schemas safely.
Benefit: Polyglot persistence
Choose the best database per service: document, relational, key-value, etc.
Consequence: Coordination needed
Multi-service operations require protocols or events instead of a single transaction.
Cost: Operational overhead
More datastores mean more backups, monitoring, and schema management tasks.
Example
ProductService: document DB for flexible attributes. PaymentService: relational DB for transactional integrity. Orders: its own store for order lifecycle tracking.
Checklist
  1. Define canonical owner for each data item.
  2. Expose minimal read APIs or events.
  3. Plan replication as eventual consistency.
  4. Make updates idempotent where needed.
Key Takeaway

Owner-controlled databases keep services autonomous but move coordination responsibilities into the architecture.

screens.title: Strong consistency vs Eventual consistency
screens.narratorSegment: Consistency is about what reads return after writes. Strong consistency guarantees that any read will return the most recent write; this is what single-database ACID transactions give you. Eventual consistency guarantees that if no new updates are made, replicas will converge on the same value after some time. The trade-off is real: strong consistency simplifies reasoning and correctness but can limit scalability and availability when applied across distributed services. Eventual consistency enables higher throughput and partition tolerance but requires accepting short windows of divergence. A useful analogy: think of a bank account balance (strong consistency desirable) versus a social media feed like counts (eventual consistency acceptable). In the bank case, a temporary divergence could lead to financial loss; in the social feed case, a few milliseconds of lag is tolerable. Practically, many systems mix both models: use strong consistency for critical operations like payments and eventual consistency for read-heavy, non-critical views. Misconception to avoid: eventual consistency is not 'inconsistent forever' — it is predictable and correct if designed with compensations and reconciliation. Example: replicate product stock to a read-optimized cache that is eventually updated; validate availability at purchase time with the owning inventory service. Key takeaway: choose the consistency model that matches correctness and availability requirements.

keyIdea.text: Strong consistency eases correctness but limits availability; eventual consistency boosts scalability and needs reconciliation and compensations where correctness matters.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Consistency Models
Strong consistency
Reads always return the latest write. Best for financial operations and critical state changes.
  • Guarantees immediate correctness after a write.
  • Often requires coordination that can reduce availability.
  • Use when business correctness cannot tolerate divergence.
Analogy
Bank balance updates should be strongly consistent to avoid overdraws.
Eventual consistency
Replicas converge over time. Good for high-read scenarios and when temporary divergence is tolerable.
  • Enables higher availability and performance at scale.
  • Requires reconciliation and careful error handling.
  • Design compensations or validation for operations that must be correct.
Analogy
Social media counts may lag briefly but correct themselves quickly.
Example
Validation at purchase time: even with eventual consistency in caches, validate stock with InventoryService for the final commit.
Misconception
Eventual consistency is not permanent inconsistency; it requires designed convergence and compensations.
Key Takeaway

Match consistency to the business requirement: use strong when correctness is essential, eventual when latency and availability matter more.

screens.title: Distributed transactions and two-phase commit (2PC)
screens.narratorSegment: Distributed transactions seek to extend ACID guarantees across multiple independent databases, and two-phase commit is a classic protocol for that. In practice, 2PC introduces tight coupling: participants must be online, coordinate locks, and wait for the coordinator. This blocking behavior reduces availability and increases latency, especially under partial failures. In a microservices environment where services must be independently deployable and scalable, this becomes a serious operational liability. For example, if OrderService blocks waiting for a lock in InventoryService, both services' throughput suffers. A common error is to choose 2PC for correctness without considering the operational costs: slow recovery, complex failure handling, and degraded availability. Instead, many teams accept weaker guarantees and use compensation patterns like sagas that trade strict atomicity for greater availability and simpler failure modes. That trade-off aligns with the microservices principle of autonomy: rather than forcing all services to participate in a single atomic commit, let each service commit locally and coordinate via events and compensations. Example: avoid two-phase commit across Order, Inventory, and Payment; prefer an event-driven saga that sequences local commits and handles failures via compensating transactions. Key question: which correctness requirements in your system truly need global locks, and which can be achieved with compensating workflows?

keyIdea.title: 2PC Pitfall
keyIdea.text: Two-phase commit enforces strong consistency but at the cost of availability, latency, and operational complexity in microservices.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Distributed Transactions & 2PC
Process
Two-phase commit overview
2PC coordinates multiple participants with a prepare and commit phase. It's blocking and couples availability to all participants' health.
  1. Coordinator asks participants to prepare. Participants lock resources and respond ready/not-ready.
  2. If all ready, coordinator instructs commit; otherwise instructs rollback. Participants then commit or rollback.
  3. Locks and coordination can block progress; failures require complex recovery protocols.
Why it's problematic
It reduces availability because every participant must be responsive and accept locks for the duration of the protocol.
Example scenario
An Order coordinator waits on Inventory and Payment. If Payment is slow or partitioned, the whole transaction blocks.
Alternative
Use sagas: sequence local commits and define compensating actions when steps fail.
Consideration
If strict global atomicity is absolutely required, weigh the operational costs carefully before using 2PC.
Key Takeaway

Avoid distributed ACID unless necessary; prefer sagas for multi-service business processes to improve availability and reduce coupling.

screens.title: Saga pattern: sequence of local transactions
screens.narratorSegment: A saga is a sequence of local transactions where each step updates its service's database and publishes an event that triggers the next step. Sagas avoid global locks by letting each participant commit locally and communicate through events. In the order fulfillment example, the sequence typically looks like: OrderService creates an OrderPending record and emits OrderCreated; InventoryService consumes it, reserves stock, and emits StockReserved; PaymentService consumes stock reservation, processes payment, and emits PaymentProcessed; OrderService consumes that and marks the order confirmed. If any step fails, the saga executes compensating transactions to undo prior changes — for example, if payment fails, InventoryService releases reserved stock and OrderService marks the order cancelled. Two implementation styles exist: choreography where services listen and react to events, and orchestration where a central coordinator tells services what to do. Choreography is decentralized and fits teams that prefer event-driven flows; orchestration centralizes state and can simplify complex error handling. Common mistake: forgetting to make saga steps idempotent. If events are retried, steps must safely reapply without corruption. Example: reserve stock must be repeatable or check if already reserved before acting. Key takeaway: sagas trade global atomicity for operational simplicity and availability, provided you design compensations and idempotency carefully.

keyIdea.title: Saga Overview
keyIdea.text: A saga sequences local commits and uses compensating transactions to preserve business-level atomicity without distributed locks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Saga Pattern
Pattern
Saga: sequence + compensation
Sagas coordinate by events; each step commits locally and publishes an event for the next step. Failures trigger compensations.
1. OrderService: create OrderPending and publish OrderCreated.
2. InventoryService: reserve stock and publish StockReserved.
3. PaymentService: process payment and publish PaymentProcessed.
4. OrderService: mark OrderConfirmed.
Failure example
If payment fails, PaymentService emits PaymentFailed; InventoryService releases stock; OrderService marks order cancelled.
Important constraint
Every step should be idempotent and publish clear events so retries and compensations are safe and observable.
Key Takeaway

Sagas provide a practical way to manage distributed workflows by sequencing local transactions and defining compensations to recover from failures.

screens.title: Order fulfillment saga: event sequence walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the order fulfillment saga with concrete events and the minimal data each event should carry. Step one: OrderService creates an OrderPending record and publishes an OrderCreated event with orderId, items, and total. Step two: InventoryService consumes OrderCreated, attempts to reserve stock for each item, and publishes StockReserved with reservationId and reservedItems. Step three: PaymentService consumes StockReserved and attempts payment; on success it publishes PaymentProcessed with paymentId, on failure PaymentFailed with reason. Step four: OrderService consumes PaymentProcessed to mark the order confirmed, or consumes PaymentFailed to mark it cancelled. For each event, include correlation identifiers and timestamps so operations are traceable. A concrete message example for OrderCreated might be: orderId: 42, userId: 1001, items: [{productId: 'P-9', qty: 2}], total: 120.00. Remember to make consumers idempotent: if an event is delivered twice, processing must not double-reserve stock or double-charge payment. Misconception: including every field in events is unnecessary; include the minimal data needed for the next step and a way to fetch extra data if needed. Key takeaway: design clear event shapes, correlation ids, and idempotent handlers to make sagas robust.

keyIdea.title: Event Design
keyIdea.text: Events should carry minimal necessary data, correlation ids, and be processed idempotently to enable reliable saga steps and observability.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Order Fulfillment Saga
Message examples
Minimal shapes with correlation ids and timestamps.
{
  "event": "OrderCreated",
  "orderId": 42,
  "userId": 1001,
  "items": [{ "productId": "P-9", "qty": 2 }],
  "total": 120.00,
  "correlationId": "corr-abc-123",
  "timestamp": "2026-01-01T12:00:00Z"
}

{
  "event": "StockReserved",
  "reservationId": "res-77",
  "orderId": 42,
  "reservedItems": [{ "productId": "P-9", "qty": 2 }],
  "correlationId": "corr-abc-123"
}

{
  "event": "PaymentProcessed",
  "paymentId": "pay-55",
  "orderId": 42,
  "status": "success",
  "correlationId": "corr-abc-123"
}
Guidelines
  • Include correlationId to trace the saga across services.
  • Keep events focused: send only data required by subscribers.
  • Design steps to be idempotent and safe to retry.
Misconception

screens.title: Compensating transactions and idempotency
screens.narratorSegment: When a saga step fails, compensating transactions reverse the effects of prior successful steps to restore a consistent business state. Compensations are business-level undo operations, not necessarily the inverse of a database write. For example, if PaymentService fails after InventoryService reserved stock, the compensation is for InventoryService to release the reservation, not to roll back a cross-service lock. Designing compensations requires thought: identify what state must be reversed, which actions are safe to undo, and how to signal compensations via events. Idempotency is the other critical piece: handlers must be safe to execute multiple times because events can be delivered more than once. A common pattern is to use unique request or correlation IDs and record processed IDs in the service store so duplicate messages are ignored. Example: when reserving stock, write a reservation record keyed by correlationId; if the same event arrives again, detect the existing reservation and return success. Misconception: compensations are perfect rollbacks; they are pragmatic corrections and may not restore the exact pre-transaction state, but they restore business invariants. Key takeaway: plan compensating actions and idempotency from the start; they are essential to making sagas reliable in failure scenarios.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Compensation & Idempotency
Compensating transactions
Compensations undo or correct the business effects of prior steps when a saga fails partway through.
  • Identify the business invariant to restore after failure, e.g., inventory consistency, payment reversal.
  • Compensations are triggered by failure events and executed as local transactions by the owning service.
  • They may not restore pre-transaction state perfectly but must return the system to a safe, consistent state.
Design note
Document compensating flows alongside forward flows so teams understand rollback implications.
Idempotency pattern
Use correlation IDs and processed-record tables so repeated deliveries are detected and ignored or handled safely.
Example
Reserve stock: create reservation record keyed by correlationId. If reservation exists, return success rather than duplicating reservation.
Key Takeaway

Design compensations and idempotency together to ensure sagas handle failures and retries without corrupting state.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: design a saga for user registration
screens.narratorSegment: This activity asks you to map a simple user registration into a saga. Scenario: UserService creates the account, ProfileService creates the default profile. Step one in a successful flow: UserService writes a user record and publishes UserCreated with userId and basic profile data. Step two: ProfileService consumes UserCreated, writes a profile and publishes ProfileCreated. Step three: UserService consumes ProfileCreated and marks registration complete. If ProfileService fails, ProfileCreated is not emitted; ProfileService should emit ProfileCreationFailed with a reason. On receiving that event, UserService executes a compensating action: mark the user account as creationFailed or delete the provisional user record. When designing this saga, include correlationId, timestamps, and idempotency checks for each step. For compensation, decide whether to soft-delete or hard-delete user records and document the choice. Common mistake: performing compensations that break auditability. Prefer marking records with a failure status and scheduling background cleanup so you preserve traces of what happened. Finally, define the events you would publish at each step and sketch the minimal fields required. This lab builds your ability to define forward and compensating flows clearly and safely.

keyIdea.title: Activity Goal
keyIdea.text: Practice converting a simple cross-service operation into a saga with explicit forward steps, events, and compensations while preserving idempotency and observability.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Lab: Registration Saga
Hands-on activity
Saga Design — User Registration
Outline forward flow, compensations, and events for a registration that spans UserService and ProfileService.
Successful flow
  1. UserService: create provisional user, publish UserCreated{userId, email, correlationId}.
  2. ProfileService: on UserCreated, create profile, publish ProfileCreated{profileId, userId, correlationId}.
  3. UserService: on ProfileCreated, mark registration complete.
Failure & compensation
  1. ProfileService fails and publishes ProfileCreationFailed{userId, reason, correlationId}.
  2. UserService consumes failure and executes compensating action: mark user as failed or remove provisional user depending on audit needs.
  3. Record the correlationId so retries do not duplicate work.
Event fields checklist
  • correlationId, userId, timestamp, minimal payload for next consumer.
  • Include failure reason codes to guide compensations.
Pro tip
Prefer soft-failure markers and background cleanup over immediate hard deletes to preserve auditability and simplify recovery.
Key Takeaway

Practice designing forward and compensating steps, making handlers idempotent, and preserving observability through correlation ids and timestamps.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential ideas to carry forward. First, database-per-service gives each team ownership of data, enabling independent deployment and appropriate technology choice, but it creates the need for explicit coordination. Second, consistency choices are a trade-off: strong consistency simplifies correctness but can reduce availability, while eventual consistency supports scalability and requires reconciliation. Third, the Saga pattern sequences local transactions and uses compensations to maintain business-level atomicity without distributed locks. When designing sagas, focus on clear event shapes, correlation identifiers, idempotency, and compensating actions. Avoid the temptation to force distributed ACID across services; two-phase commit introduces blocking and operational complexity that often outweigh its benefits in microservices. Instead, pick the simplest pattern that meets your correctness constraints and accept practical trade-offs. Ask yourself after every design: which invariants must be enforced immediately, and which can be achieved through eventual convergence and compensations?

Database per Service

screens.title: What to Remember

An operation that counteracts a previous successful step to maintain business invariants.
Idempotency
Design handlers so repeated events do not cause duplicate effects.

fullNarratorScript:
Managing data across microservices is one of the hardest practical problems in distributed systems. In this chapter you will learn why a shared monolithic database undermines service autonomy, what it means for each service to own its database, how different consistency models affect user experience, and a pragmatic pattern — the Saga — for coordinating multi-step business processes. We'll use the order fulfillment example to see events, local transactions, and compensating operations in action, and we'll practice designing a small saga for user registration. By the end you should be able to pick appropriate consistency levels, explain the trade-offs of database-per-service, and outline a saga that keeps the system reliable without locking all services into a single transaction. A common misconception is that distributed ACID transactions are always the safest choice; we'll explain why they often reduce availability and how sagas offer a more operationally practical alternative. Think of this chapter as a map: you will learn patterns and pitfalls so you can choose the simplest safe approach for your business needs.

By the end of this first objectives panel, you will be able to identify the core challenges of managing data in a distributed microservices environment and describe the database-per-service pattern with examples. Specifically, you will explain why a shared monolithic database causes coupling and how giving each service its own store enables independent deployment and polyglot persistence. For example, you will see how a Product service can use a document store for flexible catalogs while a Payment service uses a relational store for strict transactional guarantees. This screen also asks you to reflect on how these choices affect team boundaries, scaling, and schema evolution. A common misconception is that multiple databases make data consistency impossible; instead they require different coordination patterns. Consider how this objective changes your design conversations: do you prioritize autonomy for faster releases, or consistency for simple operations? That judgement is what these competencies aim to sharpen.

This second objectives panel deepens the practical skills: you will practice mapping a multi-service business operation into a saga, design compensating transactions, and identify required event shapes and idempotency boundaries. We will focus on a user registration activity and the order fulfillment example so you can see how events flow and which steps need retry safety. You will also learn to recognize common mistakes, such as trying to force two-phase commit across services or neglecting idempotency, and how those mistakes make systems brittle. Finally, you will learn to trade design complexity against necessity: not every multi-step operation requires a saga; sometimes simpler retry and reconciliation suffice. These competencies are about pragmatic design — choose the right amount of coordination to meet business correctness without overengineering. Learning Objectives means practice designing sagas and compensations, and learn to choose the simplest coordination mechanism that meets business needs.. In practical terms, what you'll be able to do after this chapter — part 2. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Start by contrasting two basic approaches: a single shared database for all components, and database-per-service where each microservice owns its private store. In a monolith, components read and write the same schema, so transactions are easy: a single ACID commit enforces correctness. That sounds convenient, but it tightly couples teams, deployment cycles, and schema changes. A migration or an index change can force coordinated releases across multiple teams. Conversely, database-per-service enforces strong service boundaries. Each service controls its schema, technology, and scaling, enabling independent deployments. An immediate benefit is polyglot persistence: you can pick a document database for flexible product catalogs and a relational database for payments. The trade-off is that multi-service business operations no longer fit into one ACID transaction. You must design coordination protocols and accept potential temporary inconsistencies. A common misconception is that autonomy implies data duplication is wrong; in fact, duplicating data across services is often the practical path to resilience. Example: an Order service keeps its own order records while Inventory service keeps stock counts; both may store the same product ID but each maintains the data it needs. Key takeaway: prefer autonomy for rapid delivery, but plan explicit coordination for cross-service consistency. Which boundaries in your system are worth strict coupling, and which deserve independent evolution?

Database per service means each microservice owns and controls its own private datastore; other services never access that store directly. This enforces service autonomy: each team can deploy, scale, and evolve schema without coordinating changes across unrelated teams. The benefits include loose coupling, technology choice per service (polyglot persistence), and localized performance tuning. A practical example: ProductService uses a document database to store variable product attributes and support flexible queries; PaymentService uses a relational database to rely on ACID semantics for money transfers. Importantly, ownership implies responsibility: the owning service must provide APIs or events for others to access its data. A typical misconception is that owning a private database removes the need to think about global data; it does not. You still need to design APIs, decide what to duplicate, and plan for eventual consistency when data is replicated. Also consider operational costs: multiple datastores may increase run-time maintenance and monitoring. A short checklist helps: define the canonical data owner, expose minimal read APIs or events, make replicated fields eventually consistent, and design idempotent update operations. Practical takeaway: use database-per-service to preserve team autonomy, but invest in clear contracts and monitoring so cross-service data flows remain reliable.

Consistency is about what reads return after writes. Strong consistency guarantees that any read will return the most recent write; this is what single-database ACID transactions give you. Eventual consistency guarantees that if no new updates are made, replicas will converge on the same value after some time. The trade-off is real: strong consistency simplifies reasoning and correctness but can limit scalability and availability when applied across distributed services. Eventual consistency enables higher throughput and partition tolerance but requires accepting short windows of divergence. A useful analogy: think of a bank account balance (strong consistency desirable) versus a social media feed like counts (eventual consistency acceptable). In the bank case, a temporary divergence could lead to financial loss; in the social feed case, a few milliseconds of lag is tolerable. Practically, many systems mix both models: use strong consistency for critical operations like payments and eventual consistency for read-heavy, non-critical views. Misconception to avoid: eventual consistency is not 'inconsistent forever' — it is predictable and correct if designed with compensations and reconciliation. Example: replicate product stock to a read-optimized cache that is eventually updated; validate availability at purchase time with the owning inventory service. Key takeaway: choose the consistency model that matches correctness and availability requirements.

Distributed transactions seek to extend ACID guarantees across multiple independent databases, and two-phase commit is a classic protocol for that. In practice, 2PC introduces tight coupling: participants must be online, coordinate locks, and wait for the coordinator. This blocking behavior reduces availability and increases latency, especially under partial failures. In a microservices environment where services must be independently deployable and scalable, this becomes a serious operational liability. For example, if OrderService blocks waiting for a lock in InventoryService, both services' throughput suffers. A common error is to choose 2PC for correctness without considering the operational costs: slow recovery, complex failure handling, and degraded availability. Instead, many teams accept weaker guarantees and use compensation patterns like sagas that trade strict atomicity for greater availability and simpler failure modes. That trade-off aligns with the microservices principle of autonomy: rather than forcing all services to participate in a single atomic commit, let each service commit locally and coordinate via events and compensations. Example: avoid two-phase commit across Order, Inventory, and Payment; prefer an event-driven saga that sequences local commits and handles failures via compensating transactions. Key question: which correctness requirements in your system truly need global locks, and which can be achieved with compensating workflows?

A saga is a sequence of local transactions where each step updates its service's database and publishes an event that triggers the next step. Sagas avoid global locks by letting each participant commit locally and communicate through events. In the order fulfillment example, the sequence typically looks like: OrderService creates an OrderPending record and emits OrderCreated; InventoryService consumes it, reserves stock, and emits StockReserved; PaymentService consumes stock reservation, processes payment, and emits PaymentProcessed; OrderService consumes that and marks the order confirmed. If any step fails, the saga executes compensating transactions to undo prior changes — for example, if payment fails, InventoryService releases reserved stock and OrderService marks the order cancelled. Two implementation styles exist: choreography where services listen and react to events, and orchestration where a central coordinator tells services what to do. Choreography is decentralized and fits teams that prefer event-driven flows; orchestration centralizes state and can simplify complex error handling. Common mistake: forgetting to make saga steps idempotent. If events are retried, steps must safely reapply without corruption. Example: reserve stock must be repeatable or check if already reserved before acting. Key takeaway: sagas trade global atomicity for operational simplicity and availability, provided you design compensations and idempotency carefully.

Let's walk through the order fulfillment saga with concrete events and the minimal data each event should carry. Step one: OrderService creates an OrderPending record and publishes an OrderCreated event with orderId, items, and total. Step two: InventoryService consumes OrderCreated, attempts to reserve stock for each item, and publishes StockReserved with reservationId and reservedItems. Step three: PaymentService consumes StockReserved and attempts payment; on success it publishes PaymentProcessed with paymentId, on failure PaymentFailed with reason. Step four: OrderService consumes PaymentProcessed to mark the order confirmed, or consumes PaymentFailed to mark it cancelled. For each event, include correlation identifiers and timestamps so operations are traceable. A concrete message example for OrderCreated might be: orderId: 42, userId: 1001, items: [{productId: 'P-9', qty: 2}], total: 120.00. Remember to make consumers idempotent: if an event is delivered twice, processing must not double-reserve stock or double-charge payment. Misconception: including every field in events is unnecessary; include the minimal data needed for the next step and a way to fetch extra data if needed. Key takeaway: design clear event shapes, correlation ids, and idempotent handlers to make sagas robust.

When a saga step fails, compensating transactions reverse the effects of prior successful steps to restore a consistent business state. Compensations are business-level undo operations, not necessarily the inverse of a database write. For example, if PaymentService fails after InventoryService reserved stock, the compensation is for InventoryService to release the reservation, not to roll back a cross-service lock. Designing compensations requires thought: identify what state must be reversed, which actions are safe to undo, and how to signal compensations via events. Idempotency is the other critical piece: handlers must be safe to execute multiple times because events can be delivered more than once. A common pattern is to use unique request or correlation IDs and record processed IDs in the service store so duplicate messages are ignored. Example: when reserving stock, write a reservation record keyed by correlationId; if the same event arrives again, detect the existing reservation and return success. Misconception: compensations are perfect rollbacks; they are pragmatic corrections and may not restore the exact pre-transaction state, but they restore business invariants. Key takeaway: plan compensating actions and idempotency from the start; they are essential to making sagas reliable in failure scenarios.
